note: upstream_ids are the NFRx.y IDs the traceability sensor derives from this unit's performance, security, scalability and reliability requirements. The sensor does not read observability-requirements.md, so NFR24.x, NFR25.x and NFR26.x are not derived as upstream even though this stage designs them; NFR25.3 appears because reliability-requirements.md cites it. Those blocks are designed in observability-design.md and were declared in the nfr-requirements reverse array. NFR6.1 and NFR12.1 are citations of the prior record's rules, not IDs defined here.

coverage.target: No new client dependency; D1's screens use the existing Compose stack (performance-design section 6)
Code and strings only; the 15 MB assertion is measured at the release gate, owned by D5/D6 (performance-design section 6)
Cited from the prior record: the one-statement lens resolution shape D1 preserves (performance-design section 1)
No scaling change; fixed host, two workers, no partitioning or replica (scalability-design section 1)
The signup ceiling cascade is the capacity control, which is why its counters must be datastore-backed (scalability-design section 2)
Named as a handed-forward gap: the 48-hour disposition exists, no job enforces it; D1 adds none (scalability-design section 2, logical-components section 6)
Database uniqueness on Account.phone rather than an application check (scalability-design section 3)
The decision transition is idempotent in its target state, a state-machine property rather than a lock (scalability-design section 3)
Upsert increments then compares, so two workers cannot both read a passing count (scalability-design section 3)
No service, no datastore, no scheduled job; the hand-off table in logical-components section 6 states it explicitly
The two new columns sit on tables already covered by storage encryption (security-design section 5)
Row-level security on profile, inherited unchanged: layer two of the three-layer table in security-design section 1, and the attachment point in logical-components section 2
No new SDK; the manifest allowlist and release DEX scan already fail the build (security-design section 5)
Cited from the prior record: the per-purpose SMS budget, which signup does not extend since the message it causes is an OTP
New ScopeKind members plus a second cascade builder, narrowest-first (security-design section 2)
Declaration order is evaluation order; the check runs before the transaction so a refusal writes nothing (security-design section 2)
Counters stay in the datastore; the in-process alternative is listed as a temptation D1 refuses (scalability-design section 1)
A ceiling breach is a ConflictError, so nothing in the stack treats it as retryable (reliability-design section 1)
Named members added to the closed AuthEvent enum, never a detail column (observability-design section 1, security-design section 3)
No log line or audit row carries a phone number, OTP, token, address or self-authored name; the row dataclass has no free-form string but correlation_id (observability-design section 4)
Account creation added as a named member of the closed AuthEvent vocabulary, earning its place on the same abuse profile as OTP issue (observability-design section 1)
A ceiling breach records its scope KIND and never its scope value, which is a phone number or IP prefix (observability-design section 1)
The savepoint buys the silence to the user and the critical log makes that silence acceptable; one decision, not two (observability-design section 1)

Signup returns no access or refresh token; the existing OTP path stays the one route to a session, so token rotation and reuse detection are built on one entry point (security-design section 4, Signup issues no session)
The OTP route is untouched and its existing adversarial test re-runs (security-design section 2)
The lookup is bounded in width and in rate; the opposite-properties table in security-design section 2
InvitationLens as a fourth type rather than a resolver branch; an empty list rather than a 403 (security-design sections 1 and 4)
Three-layer privacy boundary with address joining the hand-maintained field-name set (security-design section 1, logical-components section 2)
No availability target of D1's own; the Phase 1 single-host recreate posture is inherited (reliability-design section 5)
Deploy scheduling follows the existing practice, since the same deploy carries everything else (reliability-design section 5)
Additive columns make the previous image run against the new schema; Alembic runs as a distinct logged step (reliability-design section 4)
The conditional backfill, with the withdrawn-lens failure mode stated (reliability-design section 4)
Verified pg_dump to S3 with object existence and size asserted (reliability-design section 4)
Rehearsed on staging against realistic data (reliability-design section 4)
One transaction over account, profile and the conditional owner row (reliability-design section 3)
Retryability read off the error class in one place; the gateway failure deliberately leaves the account created (reliability-design sections 2 and 3)
No write path resets a decision; the transition table in reliability-design section 3
Both predicates sit on columns the query already locates, so no join and no round trip are added (performance-design section 1)
The access path is preserved, which is why the requirement is a property rather than a millisecond figure (performance-design section 1)
The invitation grant gets its own statement on its own route, because a grant is a set and a scalar returns one (performance-design section 2)
Once-per-account write with no latency budget beyond ordinary handling (performance-design section 4)
A single indexed read on a unique column; the constraint reports duplicates rather than a separate lookup (performance-design section 4)
The OTP trigger sits outside the transaction, so a slow gateway delays the code and not the account (performance-design section 4)
No cache of any kind; the permitted request-scoped memo is distinguished by where the value lives (performance-design section 3)

GET /v1/me stays counts-only; D1 changes what the counts mean and not their shape, refusing the per-lens eager fetch acceptance makes tempting (performance-design section 1, GET /v1/me stays counts-only)
Acceptance transitions written test-first per the affirmed predicate (security-design section 6)
The adversarial test must fail against today's code before the predicate lands (security-design section 6)
The authorization layer is measured as branch coverage (security-design section 6)
The audit write fails open behind a savepoint, which is why its failure must alert (reliability-design section 5, observability-design section 1)
